target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would broadly remove scheduling barriers to voting and improve access.
objection: A federal holiday designation does not, by itself, require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many workers—especially in private-sector retail and service jobs—would still face the same work-schedule barriers on Election Day.

target: AG1's assumption that a national holiday would help low-income workers.
objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately employed in hourly, inflexible jobs and are less able to take unpaid time off without losing wages or risking job consequences, so an Election Day holiday would especially fail to solve their voting-time problem and could leave them relatively worse off than higher-resourced voters.

target: AG1's claim that an Election Day holiday is an effective turnout strategy.
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday is just a symbolic label and does not change access in private workplaces.
objection: A national-holiday law can be written to require employers to provide sufficient time to vote, so it need not be merely symbolic; if paired with time-off obligations, it would reduce work-schedule barriers in private workplaces too.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged by a holiday.
objection: If the policy guarantees time to vote during the workday, it specifically helps low-income hourly workers who are most constrained by wages and rigid schedules, rather than disadvantaging them.

target: AG1's response that the holiday can be paired with employer time-off requirements.
objection: A federal designation of Election Day as a holiday does not by itself require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so retail and service workplaces would likely stay open and many private-sector workers would still face the same scheduling constraints.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would not disadvantage low-income workers.
objection: Because low-income workers are concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs with little scheduling flexibility, they are less able to take unpaid time off and therefore are the most likely to remain constrained by work on Election Day.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is a strong turnout reform.
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout lever, so it is an unreliable way to substantially improve participation.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday's weaker performance compared with other reforms defeats it.
objection: The core justification for the holiday is that it removes concrete scheduling barriers, not that it must beat every other reform on turnout in isolation; a reform can still be worthwhile if it improves access even when not the single strongest turnout lever.

target: AG2's assumption that workplaces would simply remain open and unchanged on a federal holiday.
objection: On federal holidays many workplaces reduce hours or close, and schools/daycare often close as well, so a national Election Day holiday would give many people real time away from work and care obligations to vote.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would not help families with school or childcare barriers.
objection: Because school and daycare closures or reduced operations on a federal holiday lower childcare barriers, the holiday would particularly help parents whose voting access is constrained by school schedules.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged rather than helped.
objection: If the holiday reduces work and school constraints as intended, it is not likely to disadvantage low-income workers relative to higher-resourced voters; instead it addresses key constraints faced by low-income families.

target: AG2's claim that weekend/holiday elections are not a workable model.
objection: Many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, showing that election timing on non-workdays is feasible in established democracies and can be built into civic routines.

target: AG2's claim that bipartisan support does not matter because the policy is still merely symbolic.
objection: Broad cross-party support indicates the measure is politically feasible and can be implemented with the practical details needed to address the time constraints that motivate support, rather than being left as a symbolic label.

target: AG2's claim that early voting and absentee voting do not make a holiday helpful.
objection: Because most jurisdictions already offer early in-person and/or mail/absentee voting across a broader voting period, giving workers extra accessible days through a holiday can help them use those options without needing to be off work specifically on Election Day.

target: AG1's claim that broader voting options mean the holiday helps low-income workers more than it hurts them.
objection: Even with early in-person and mail voting, workers may still need time on specific days to vote early or handle mail/absentee logistics, and low-income hourly workers still have less flexibility to do that; therefore the holiday does not reliably solve their access problem and may still leave them disadvantaged relative to higher-resourced voters.

target: AG2's claim that early/mail voting means low-income workers are still disadvantaged.
objection: Early in-person voting is often on weekends or in evening hours, and mail/absentee voting can be done at home, so the broader voting window can reduce work-schedule barriers for hourly workers without requiring Election Day off specifically.

target: AG2's assumption that holiday time will not create meaningful extra access for hourly workers.
objection: Many retail/service employers reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so low-income hourly workers often do have less regular work time on the holiday and can use that time to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday also solves registration and ballot-access bottlenecks.
objection: Voting requires more than time off; it also requires being properly registered and meeting registration and ballot deadlines, which a holiday does not automatically fix.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday helps low-income voters proportionally on registration and ballot access.
objection: Low-income voters face greater friction in meeting administrative requirements like documentation and deadlines, and a holiday does not directly solve those non-time bottlenecks, so it is less likely to improve access for them proportionally.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday cannot help with registration and ballot-access prerequisites.
objection: Many of those prerequisites involve time-sensitive administrative tasks that overlap work and school hours, so protected holiday time can help people complete the needed steps and meet deadlines rather than only helping them get to a polling place.

target: AG1's argument that a single holiday day can meaningfully fix registration and ballot-access problems.
objection: Many registration and ballot-access deadlines occur before Election Day, and some prerequisites depend on government offices or service providers operating during normal business hours; a one-day holiday on Election Day does not change those earlier deadlines or processing windows.

target: AG2's claim that preregistration problems are mostly outside the voter's control.
objection: Many registration and ballot-access tasks still require voter-controlled steps like gathering documents, completing forms, and attending appointments during business hours, so protected time away from work or school can materially reduce those bottlenecks.

target: AG1's argument that holiday time can fix documentation and eligibility problems.
objection: Some bottlenecks depend on obtaining or verifying records that take more than one day because of waiting periods, fees, and processing by outside entities, so a one-day Election Day holiday cannot reliably eliminate those documentation and eligibility barriers.

target: AG2's claim that documentation/eligibility bottlenecks are mostly beyond the holiday's reach.
objection: Many bottlenecks are driven not only by outside processing but also by voters' ability to do deadline-sensitive tasks like gathering documents, filling out forms, and making appointments during business hours, and holiday time helps with those voter-controlled steps.

target: AG1's claim that holiday time can fix receipt and processing problems around deadlines.
objection: Many registration and ballot-access steps must be received and processed by election officials by a deadline, and holiday-related reductions in government or postal operations can delay receipt and processing rather than speed them up, so the holiday does not reliably clear those bottlenecks.

target: AG2's claim that only targeted reforms count as reliable access measures.
objection: Some ballot-access deadlines and cure windows fall on or near Election Day, so having a holiday then gives constrained voters extra time to complete and submit key steps and can reliably reduce those deadline-near bottlenecks.

target: AG1's claim that federal holiday closures create usable time for low-income parents and workers.
objection: Holiday closures do not automatically create usable time, because low-income workers may still have to work on a federal holiday without paid leave and may also lack affordable childcare, so the holiday does not reliably relieve the practical constraints that block registration and ballot-access tasks.

target: AG2's broader claim that federal holidays do not provide real additional time for workers and parents.
objection: On federal holidays many schools, daycare facilities, and workplaces reduce hours or close, creating more actual time off and scheduling flexibility for hourly workers and parents than on a normal weekday.

target: AG1's claim that holiday closures help low-income parents complete voter tasks.
objection: Low-income parents often cannot stay home because they still have to work and may lack alternative childcare, so holiday closures do not reliably give them the time needed to complete voter-registration or ballot-access steps.

target: AG2's claim that schools/workplaces probably stay fully operating and give no added time.
objection: Many schools/daycare centers and a large share of workplaces reduce hours or close on federal holidays, so a national Election Day holiday would create additional usable time for low-income hourly workers and parents to complete voter-controlled steps.
